items.title: Q1 · Dec 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: ____ the very word is like a bell To toll me back from thee to my sole self ! Which word ?

structured.lead:
____ the very word is like a bell
To toll me back from thee to my sole self !
Which word ?
structured.options_hint: Bird Immortal Forlorn Fancy

items.explanation: These lines open the eighth and final stanza of John Keats's 'Ode to a Nightingale' (1819). Echoing the word 'forlorn' from the end of Stanza 7 ('perilous seas, in faery lands forlorn'), the word acts like a tolling bell that pulls the speaker back from imaginative transport to his solitary self.

structured.options_hint: John Donne, alliteration Robert Herrick,

items.explanation: In his devotional collection The Temple (1633), Metaphysical poet George Herbert famously used pattern poetry (carmina figurata) in 'The Altar' and 'Easter-Wings,' arranging line lengths and typographic space on the page so that the printed poems visually resemble an altar and pairs of wings.

items.title: Q3 · Dec 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: Units V–X: Language, English in India, Cultural Studies, Criticism, Theory & Research · Unit VIII: Literary Criticism
items.stem: No, no thou hast not felt the lapse of hours ! For what wears out the life of mortal men ? 'Tis that repeated shocks, again, again, Exhaust the energy of strongest souls And numb the elastic powers … Who does the poet address here ?

structured.lead:
No, no thou hast not felt the lapse of hours !
For what wears out the life of mortal men ?
'Tis that repeated shocks, again, again,
Exhaust the energy of strongest souls
And numb the elastic powers …
Who does the poet address here ?
structured.options_hint: The Scholar Gipsy Telemachus The Nightin

items.explanation: These lines are from Matthew Arnold's pastoral elegy 'The Scholar-Gipsy' (1853). The speaker addresses the legendary seventeenth-century Oxford scholar who joined a band of gypsies, contrasting his ageless, single-minded quest with the exhausting 'sick hurry and divided aims' of modern Victorian life.

structured.options_hint: Thomas Parnell Alexander Pope Joseph Add

items.explanation: Joseph Addison was a prominent Whig writer and member of the rival Kit-Cat Club. The Tory Scriblerus Club, founded in 1714 to satirize pedantry and 'false tastes in learning,' comprised Alexander Pope, Jonathan Swift, John Gay, Thomas Parnell, John Arbuthnot, and Robert Harley.

structured.lead:
_______ is a theological term brought into literary criticism by
_______
structured.options_hint: Entelechy, St. Augustine Ambiguity, Will

items.explanation: James Joyce adapted the Christian theological term 'epiphany' (the manifestation of Christ's divinity to the Magi) into modernist literary criticism in Stephen Hero (written 1904–1906) to denote a sudden spiritual manifestation in which the 'whatness' (quidditas) of an ordinary object or moment is revealed.

items.stem: ________ the Almighty Power Hurled headlong flaming from th' Ethereal Sky, With hideous ruin and combustion down To bottomless perdition, there to dwell In Adamantine Chains and penal Fire Who durst defy th' Omnipotent to Arms. (Paradise Lost, I.44-49.) Choose the appropriate word

items.explanation: In Book I, lines 44–49 of John Milton's Paradise Lost, the sentence begins with the objective pronoun 'Him' ('Him the Almighty Power / Hurled headlong flaming from th' Ethereal Sky'), using Latinate inverted syntax where 'Him' (Satan) is the direct object of the verb 'Hurled.'

items.title: Q11 · Dec 2013 (Paper II)
items.meta: British Romantic Period · Unit II: Poetry · Samuel Taylor Coleridge
items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a quest narrative ?

structured.lead: Which of the following is NOT a quest narrative ?
structured.options_hint: Shelley's Alastor Byron's Manfred Coleri

items.explanation: Samuel Taylor Coleridge's unfinished Gothic poem Christabel (1797–1800) is a supernatural tale of demonic seduction set at Sir Leoline's castle rather than a journey or quest narrative, whereas Shelley's Alastor, Byron's Manfred, and Keats's Endymion all center on Romantic protagonists pursuing a metaphysical or ideal quest.

structured.options_hint: Corah Shimei Zimri Achitophel

items.explanation: In John Dryden's political satire Absalom and Achitophel (1681), these lines describe 'Shimei' (lines 620–621), the biblical persona representing Slingsby Bethel, the fanatically republican Whig Sheriff of London who was notorious for his extreme parsimony and stingy kitchen.

structured.lead:
Here is a list of early English plays imitating Greek and Latin plays.
Pick the odd one out
structured.options_hint: Gorboduc Tamburlaine Ralph Roister Doist

items.explanation: Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine the Great (c. 1587) is a romantic Elizabethan blank-verse tragedy that defies classical unities and models. By contrast, Gorboduc (1561) imitated Senecan tragedy, while Ralph Roister Doister and Gammer Gurton's Needle imitated Roman comedies by Plautus and Terence.

items.explanation: Mistakenly substituting a similar-sounding word with a ludicrously different meaning—such as saying 'congenital food' instead of 'continental food'—is a malapropism, named after Mrs. Malaprop in Richard Brinsley Sheridan's comedy The Rivals (1775).

items.explanation: The concluding couplet of Robert Graves's poem 'In Broken Images' reverses the key nouns in a criss-cross ABBA pattern ('confusion of his understanding' / 'understanding of my confusion'), which is a textbook example of chiasmus (specifically antimetabole).

items.explanation: Coined by Victorian critic John Ruskin in Modern Painters (1856), 'pathetic fallacy' is the attribution of human emotions, actions, or animate behaviour—such as 'leaves dancing'—to inanimate nature.

structured.lead:
Identify the incorrect description/s of "Sprung Rhythm" from the following :
1. This rhythm causes ideas to spring in our minds – hence Sprung Rhythm.
2. In Sprung Rhythm the feet are of equal length.
3. A foot may have one to four syllables in Sprung Rhythm.
4. Its metre is derived from the metre of Anglo-Saxon poetry which was based on accent and linked by alliteration.
structured.options_hint: 4 is incorrect. 1 & 4 are incorrect. 3 i

items.explanation: Statement 1 is incorrect: G.M. Hopkins coined the term 'Sprung Rhythm' to describe a stress-timed metre in which each foot begins with a stressed syllable followed by zero to three unstressed syllables (1 to 4 syllables total, of equal musical duration, akin to Anglo-Saxon accentual verse), not because it 'causes ideas to spring in our minds'.

items.explanation: In the Third Essay ('Archetypal Criticism: Theory of Myths') of Anatomy of Criticism (1957), Northrop Frye identifies four 'mythoi' or generic narrative plots corresponding to the four seasons: the comic (spring), the romantic (summer), the tragic (autumn), and the ironic/satiric (winter). 'The lyric' is not one of the four generic plots.
